Software engineering tasks are rarely unconstrained objectives.
Developers ask agents not only to fix the bug, but also
to preserve APIs, reproduce before patching, run specific tests, avoid prohibited tools, and report what was actually
For coding agents, success is therefore not merely to solve the task, but to solve it under explicit engineering

The ANCHOR taxonomy was not designed purely from an a priori schema.
Instead, we started from grounded open-label
annotation over real developer interactions with coding agents, including task instructions, inline review comments,
and post-hoc feedback on agent trajectories.
Senior software engineers then iteratively clustered near-duplicate labels,
Five design principles guided this process.
the taxonomy should cover the major engineering constraint
types that appear in practice, so that real developer instructions map into it with minimal residue.
each leaf should admit concrete, testable instantiations with stable pass conditions
under either rule-based or LLM-based evaluation.
fine-grained diagnostic analysis at the leaf level and coarse-grained reporting at the category level.
The current release instantiates this design as a three-level hierarchy with 10 top-level categories, 34 mid-level sub-
At a coarse level, these groups capture complementary dimensions of engineering
process- and trajectory-level constraints (C1–C2), patch- and implementation-level constraints (C3–C5),
environment and system-boundary constraints (C6–C8), and validation and reporting requirements (C9–C10).
categories are the smallest operational unit:
each is intended to capture a semantically coherent developer requirement
that can be instantiated into task-grounded constraints and evaluated with relatively stable verification logic.
In practice, we prioritise instances with (i) a usable execution environment, (ii) sufficient
task and repository context to support downstream constraint selection, (iii) moderate patch complexity rather than
trivial micro-edits or very long-horizon changes, and (iv) broad coverage across programming languages and repository
